lectures.title: Users of AI: bias, technosolutionism, practice, explanation and contestation
lectures.why: Answers the sample question “critique OpenAI’s purely technical FAT document” and any question about human oversight, explanations or appeals.

parts.title: Part 1 — Why users matter; the state of AI bias

ideas.en: Studying users matters because we are all users, because it maintains trust in institutions, because it reveals hindrances, non-use cases and grounds for discrimination, because it brings models closer to “metrological realism”, and because it helps operationalise regulation.
ideas.vi: Vì sao quan tâm người dùng: chúng ta đều là người dùng; giữ niềm tin vào thể chế; phát hiện trở ngại, trường hợp không dùng, căn cứ phân biệt đối xử; giúp mô hình gần “hiện thực đo lường”; giúp vận hành hoá luật.

ideas.en: COMPAS (ProPublica, 2016) is the flagship AI-bias case: a recidivism score that displaced a debate from law and criminology to the public sphere, where data science and criminology talked past each other.
ideas.vi: COMPAS (ProPublica 2016): vụ điển hình về thiên lệch AI — điểm nguy cơ tái phạm ở Mỹ. Đẩy tranh luận từ luật/tội phạm học ra công chúng; hai đấu trường (khoa học dữ liệu vs tội phạm học) ít nói chuyện với nhau; quy tắc thống kê (actuarial) vs AI; một bài báo truyền thông có tác động học thuật khổng lồ.

ideas.en: Debiasing has mixed results (Bolukbasi et al. 2016; Prost et al. 2021 — sometimes more bias); fairness definitions remain dated, not sociologically sound and rarely intersectional.
ideas.vi: Giới hạn của “khử thiên lệch”: kết quả lẫn lộn, có khi còn thiên lệch hơn; định nghĩa công bằng lỗi thời, không vững về xã hội học, hiếm khi tính đến giao thoa (intersectionality: vd. phụ nữ da màu).

ideas.en: Algocracy is the way societies and governments use and deploy algorithmic systems to govern; bias debates reinforce the need to discuss it.
ideas.vi: Algocracy (“thuật toán trị”): cách xã hội và chính phủ dùng hệ thống thuật toán để cai trị.

ideas.en: The “fair AI vs radical AI” tension is that cases like SyRI (Netherlands welfare fraud), SCHUFA (credit scoring), CNAF (French welfare fraud), ETIAS (EU borders) and Clearview AI (facial recognition) question the point of a fair algorithm that is not attached to deeper change.
ideas.vi: Căng thẳng “AI công bằng” vs “AI cấp tiến”: các vụ SyRI (Hà Lan, gian lận phúc lợi), SCHUFA (chấm điểm tín dụng), CNAF/CAF (Pháp, gian lận phúc lợi), ETIAS (biên giới EU), Clearview AI (nhận diện khuôn mặt) → một thuật toán “công bằng” có ích gì nếu không gắn với thay đổi sâu hơn (Kalluri 2020; Keyes 2020), khi bất công bị cộng dồn (Eidelson 2021), và cần lòng trắc ẩn trong thiết kế (Vaccaro 2021).

parts.title: Part 2 — Technosolutionism

ideas.en: The mulching proposal (Keyes, Hutson & Durbin, CHI 2019) is a satire that applies Fairness, Accountability and Transparency to an algorithm turning elderly people into slurry — showing that FAT can “improve” a system whose purpose is unacceptable.
ideas.vi: “Đề xuất nghiền” (Keyes và cs. 2019) — bài châm biếm: áp dụng khung Công bằng–Trách nhiệm–Minh bạch (FAT) cho thuật toán biến người già thành thức ăn. Làm nó “công bằng” (demographic parity), “có trách nhiệm” (10 giây để phản đối + người giám sát), “minh bạch” (biển “khu vực nghiền”, website mulchme.com). Bài học: FAT không đặt câu hỏi về MỤC ĐÍCH thì biện minh được cho bất cứ thứ gì.
ideas.tip: Use it to critique any “purely technical” fairness/transparency document.

ideas.en: Technosolutionism is the idea that technology is a necessary part of the solution to a given problem; it leads to post-hoc rationalisation and out-of-touch technical fixes, and is a problem for democratic processes (Nemitz, 2023).
ideas.vi: Chủ nghĩa giải pháp công nghệ: tin rằng công nghệ nhất thiết phải là một phần của lời giải → hợp lý hoá sau khi đã quyết, giải pháp xa rời thực tế, nguy hại cho tiến trình dân chủ (Nemitz 2023). Xem thêm “bẫy trừu tượng hoá” (Selbst và cs. 2018).

ideas.en: Tech neutrality vs tech politics is the debate between seeing technology as a neutral tool and seeing it as political; discussing only uses reduces the debate to experts (Covid tracing: debate on privacy, not on Bluetooth’s inadequacy).
ideas.vi: Công nghệ trung lập vs công nghệ là chính trị: chỉ bàn “cách dùng” khiến cuộc tranh luận thành chuyện của chuyên gia — vd. app truy vết Covid: tranh cãi về quyền riêng tư, trong khi câu hỏi “Bluetooth có đo được tiếp xúc không?” bị bỏ qua.

ideas.en: Typical lobbying arguments are “if we don’t do it, others will”, “there will be a brain drain”, “regulation will thwart innovation” and “the next version will solve the problems of this one”.
ideas.vi: Lập luận vận động hành lang điển hình: “mình không làm thì người khác làm”; “chảy máu chất xám”; “quản lý sẽ bóp chết đổi mới”; “phiên bản sau sẽ sửa lỗi phiên bản này”. Nhận diện và phản biện chúng.

parts.title: Part 3 — Algorithms in practice

ideas.en: “Algorithms in practice” (Christin) is an ethnography (2011–2015, ~100 interviews) of judges/lawyers using defendant-scoring tools and web journalists using trend-mining analytics, comparing discourses with practices.
ideas.vi: Christin – “Thuật toán trong thực tế”: nghiên cứu dân tộc học 2011–2015, ~100 phỏng vấn, hai nhóm: giới luật (Paris/New York, công cụ chấm điểm bị cáo) và nhà báo mạng (công cụ dò xu hướng). Hỏi: diễn ngôn khác thực hành ra sao?

ideas.en: An expert field (Bourdieu) is a group sharing belief in the legitimacy of specific knowledge as a basis for intervening in public affairs; law has strong entry barriers and is non-profit, journalism has almost none and is profit-oriented.
ideas.vi: Trường chuyên gia (Bourdieu): nhóm cùng tin vào tính chính danh của một dạng tri thức để can thiệp vào việc công. Luật: rào cản gia nhập cao (thi luật sư), phi lợi nhuận, dè dặt với công nghệ, gắn quyết định với bản sắc. Báo chí: gần như không rào cản, vì lợi nhuận, thích công nghệ và tính tức thời.

ideas.en: Decoupling (Meyer & Rowan, 1977) is the separation between management discourse (“the tool is deployed”) and employees’ actual practice (the tool is ignored or resisted).
ideas.vi: Tách rời (decoupling): diễn ngôn quản lý (“công cụ đã triển khai thành công”) tách khỏi thực hành của nhân viên (bỏ qua hoặc chống lại công cụ). “Đã áp dụng” ≠ “được dùng thật”.

ideas.en: Buffering is the set of responses that shield work from algorithms: foot-dragging (ignoring outputs, putting them at the end of reports), gaming (clickbait titles, choosing cases) and open critique.
ideas.vi: Đệm chắn (buffering): lề mề (lờ kết quả, để cuối báo cáo), lách luật/gaming (giật tít, chọn giờ đăng, chọn vụ án), phê phán công khai (tiêu chí “thành công” của thuật toán lệch với tiêu chí của nghề). → dịch chuyển phán đoán chủ quan và lượng hoá xã hội.

ideas.en: Algorithmic imaginaries (Bucher, 2016) are “ways of thinking about what algorithms are, what they should be and how they function”; journalists question the tool’s goal, while courts openly call the tools “crude”.
ideas.vi: Hình dung về thuật toán (Bucher 2016): cách nghĩ thuật toán là gì, nên là gì. Nhà báo không nghi ngờ công cụ nhưng lưỡng lự về mục đích của nó; toà án thì công khai chê “thô thiển”, phê phán công cụ vì lợi nhuận, và thiếu án lệ khiến thay đổi chậm.

ideas.en: The Cour de cassation case is an in-house named-entity-recognition system for anonymising court decisions, annotated by civil servants: training never ends (a permanent team), the AI is called “the software”, becomes an absent colleague, and annotators mobilise empathy for readers.
ideas.vi: Toà Phá án Pháp: hệ nhận dạng thực thể (NER) để ẩn danh bản án, do công chức tự gán nhãn trong 2 năm; KHÔNG BAO GIỜ hết huấn luyện (thành đội thường trực); không gọi là “AI” mà là “phần mềm”; thành “đồng nghiệp vắng mặt”; người gán nhãn dùng sự thấu cảm để bản án vẫn dễ hiểu. Ví dụ đẹp cho “verification never goes away”.

parts.title: Part 4 — Explanations and contestation

ideas.en: A good explanation is selective, contrastive and dialogic (Miller), ideally producing a “complexity drop” (Dessalles); it must fit its audience — experts, laypeople or regulators.
ideas.vi: Giải thích tốt: có chọn lọc, mang tính đối chiếu (“vì sao A mà không phải B?”), có đối thoại (Miller); tạo ra “sự giảm độ phức tạp” (Dessalles). Phải hợp với người nghe: chuyên gia, người thường, cơ quan quản lý.

ideas.en: The four purposes of an explanation are descriptive, explanatory, normative (justification) and contestable (giving grounds to challenge).
ideas.vi: Bốn mục đích giải thích: mô tả (descriptive), giải thích (explanatory), chuẩn tắc/biện minh (normative — “vì sao như thế là đúng”), có thể phản bác (contestable — cho người ta căn cứ để khiếu nại). Ví dụ của giảng viên: chấm điểm thi — “câu 1 được 2 điểm” là mô tả; “vì sao câu trả lời chưa đạt” là biện minh.

ideas.en: The right to contest AI (Kaminski & Urban, 2021) is an individual right mimicking due process, which already fits the GDPR framework (Art. 22(3)) but puts the onus on individuals.
ideas.vi: Quyền phản đối AI (Kaminski & Urban 2021): quyền cá nhân mô phỏng “thủ tục tố tụng công bằng”; đã khớp với GDPR (Đ.22(3): quyền có sự can thiệp của con người, bày tỏ quan điểm, phản đối quyết định) — nhưng đặt gánh nặng lên vai từng cá nhân.

ideas.en: Contestation aims at citizen empowerment, acceptability of decisions, better system development and preventing gaming; its limits are that it does not fix information asymmetry or power imbalance and people fight only for their own case.
ideas.vi: Mục tiêu: trao quyền công dân, quyết định dễ chấp nhận, cải thiện hệ thống, chống lách luật. Giới hạn: không xoá bất cân xứng thông tin & quyền lực; mỗi người chỉ đấu tranh cho trường hợp của mình (tốn thời gian, tiền). Contestability = “bước ngoặt chính trị” của explainability.

ideas.en: The contestation matrix crosses individual ↔ collective with descriptive ↔ normative: an explanation (individual, descriptive), a justification (individual, normative), and deliberation or public-scrutiny tools such as the DSA transparency database, NGOs (La Quadrature du Net) or the Défenseur des droits (collective).
ideas.vi: Ma trận phản đối: trục cá nhân ↔ tập thể × mô tả ↔ chuẩn tắc. Cá nhân–mô tả: giải thích; cá nhân–chuẩn tắc: biện minh; tập thể: tranh luận công khai trước khi triển khai, cơ sở dữ liệu minh bạch DSA, NGO (La Quadrature du Net gom các vụ việc ra toà), Thanh tra quyền (Défenseur des droits) — trên lý thuyết, nhưng thiếu kinh phí.

ideas.en: Contestable AI by design (Alfrink et al., 2023) uses Value-Sensitive Design to build contestability loops into public AI, combining procedural and substantive, descriptive and normative aspects.
ideas.vi: Thiết kế AI có thể phản đối (Alfrink và cs. 2023): dùng thiết kế nhạy cảm giá trị (VSD) để đưa “vòng lặp phản đối” vào AI công; luật là một chuyện, thiết kế để khuyến khích phản đối là chuyện khác. Một khiếu nại tốt phải khả thi cho người dùng VÀ cho cơ quan (ví dụ cực đoan: bấm nút → giáo viên viết báo cáo 50 trang; hay chỉ nhận thư tay lúc nửa đêm thứ Sáu).

format.summary: 10 questions: 6 long (one A4 page each) + 4 short (all four on one A4 page). Plan 7 pages of writing.
rows: Concept + mechanism + case + concrete measure + trade-off
Exact names from the slides (teacher: “just put the names”)
order: Do the 4 short questions first (≈ 10 points that the teachers say are “free” if you know the names) — it warms up your memory.
Then the long questions in order of confidence. Never leave one blank: the 5-block skeleton with course concepts already earns the passing points.
Write the block labels small in the margin (F, A1, A2, A3, R) so you keep to one page.
teacher_hints: Framing: “there will be at least one question about framing” — always state your framing and what it hides.
Short questions: “give three examples of methods… just put the names… five questions like this = 10 points”.
SCHUFA trap: a human who always follows the score does not make the decision “not automated”.
Labour: never write only “human in the loop” — say who, which contract, how paid, internal or external.
Normative choices are allowed and expected “as long as you explain them”. Trade-offs matter more than the solution.
Scientific independent panel = researchers, independent from the Commission; non-scientists or Commission staff are out of scope.

long.label: F
long.title: Frame (3–4 lines, ~40 words)
long.en: Restate who asks, what system, for what purpose. State your framing (wide sociotechnical, not only the model) and your normative choice (which value you prioritise).
long.vi: Đặt khung: ai hỏi, hệ thống gì, mục đích gì; nói rõ mình nhìn rộng (xã hội–kỹ thuật) và chọn ưu tiên giá trị nào.

long.label: A1
long.title: Argument 1 (~65 words)
long.en: Claim → course concept (named) → mechanism in THIS case → concrete measure.
long.vi: Luận điểm 1: khẳng định → khái niệm của môn → cơ chế trong tình huống này → biện pháp cụ thể.

long.label: A2
long.title: Argument 2 (~65 words)
long.en: Same pattern, a different lecture (e.g. law if A1 was sociology).
long.vi: Luận điểm 2: cùng cấu trúc, lấy từ bài giảng khác.

long.label: A3
long.title: Argument 3 (~65 words)
long.en: Same pattern; ideally the “hidden” dimension: workers, users, contestation or materiality.
long.vi: Luận điểm 3: chiều “bị che giấu”: người lao động, người dùng, khiếu nại, tài nguyên.

long.label: R
long.title: Recommendation + trade-off (4–5 lines, ~50 words)
long.en: Decision (deploy / conditional / do not deploy), who is responsible, which evidence, revision or stop trigger, and the cost of your choice.
long.vi: Kết luận: quyết định, ai chịu trách nhiệm, bằng chứng nào, khi nào xem lại/dừng, và cái giá của lựa chọn.

short.label: D
short.title: Define in one sentence
short.en: “X is …” — the definition from the slide.

short.label: N
short.title: Name the items asked
short.en: Exact names, numbered (1) (2) (3), each with ≤ 1 line.
short.vi: Liệt kê đúng tên, đánh số.

short.label: E
short.title: One example or author
short.en: A course case or author anchors the answer (Tubaro 2020, SCHUFA, COMPAS…).
short.vi: Một ví dụ/tác giả của môn.

items.en: The question asks whether {ACTOR} should use {SYSTEM} in order to {PURPOSE}.
items.vi: Mở bài: nhắc lại câu hỏi.

items.en: I frame {SYSTEM} as a sociotechnical system rather than as a model: it includes the data, the operators ({USERS}), the hidden workers ({WORKERS}), the institution and the people affected ({AFFECTED}).
items.vi: Tuyên bố đóng khung rộng.

items.en: A narrow framing — {NARROW} — would make the problem look purely technical; a wider framing — {WIDE} — makes visible who bears the risks.
items.vi: So sánh hai cách đóng khung (câu “ăn điểm” framing).

items.en: My normative choice is to prioritise {VALUE}; I explain below what this choice costs.
items.vi: Nêu lựa chọn chuẩn tắc.

items.en: The course concept of [CONCEPT] (author, year) helps here: [CONCEPT] is [definition].
items.vi: Giới thiệu khái niệm + tác giả.

items.en: This matters in this case because {SYSTEM} directly shapes {DECISION}.
items.vi: Nối khái niệm với tình huống.

items.en: As in {CASE}, the risk is not only technical error but {HARM}.
items.vi: Dẫn tiền lệ của môn.

items.en: Under the AI Act, {SYSTEM} is an AI system because it infers outputs from its inputs; given its purpose, it is {AIACT}.
items.vi: Phân loại AI Act.

items.en: {ACTOR} acts as a deployer (or as a provider if it develops the system or puts it into service under its own name), so it must ensure human oversight, follow the instructions of use, keep logs and, as a public body, carry out a fundamental-rights impact assessment.
items.vi: Vai trò provider/deployer + nghĩa vụ.

items.en: Because {DATA} are processed, the GDPR requires one lawful basis and all the principles — in particular purpose limitation, data minimisation and storage limitation — and a DPIA before deployment.
items.vi: Câu GDPR dùng cho mọi tình huống có dữ liệu cá nhân.

items.en: Placing a human in the loop is not enough: following the SCHUFA ruling (CJEU, 2023), if {USERS} systematically follow the output, {DECISION} is in fact automated and Article 22 GDPR applies.
items.vi: Câu “bẫy SCHUFA” — học thuộc.

items.en: Oversight is meaningful only if {USERS} have the time, the information, the authority and no penalty for overriding the system; I would measure the override rate and observe actual practice (decoupling, Meyer & Rowan).
items.vi: Điều kiện giám sát thật + cách kiểm chứng.

items.en: Behind {SYSTEM} there are {WORKERS}: following Tubaro et al. (2020), they act as trainers (labelling data), verifiers (checking outputs) and sometimes imitators (doing what is sold as automatic).
items.vi: Ba vai trò lao động.

items.en: {ACTOR} should state who these workers are, how they are contracted, how much they are effectively paid and whether they are internal or subcontracted, and put these conditions in the procurement contract.
items.vi: Câu giảng viên dặn: ai, hợp đồng, trả bao nhiêu, nội bộ hay thuê ngoài.

items.en: An explanation is only useful if it is adapted to {AFFECTED}: selective, contrastive and actionable, not a technical dump of model weights.
items.vi: Giải thích phù hợp người nghe.

items.en: {AFFECTED} need a real contestation route — {CONTEST} — but individual appeals do not solve information asymmetry, so I add a collective channel (independent authority, NGOs, published statistics).
items.vi: Phản đối cá nhân + tập thể.

items.en: Before optimising fairness metrics, we must ask whether {SYSTEM} is legitimate at all: as the mulching proposal shows, fairness, accountability and transparency can make an unacceptable purpose look acceptable.
items.vi: Câu “mulching”.

items.en: A less intrusive alternative — {ALT} — should be compared, including its environmental and labour costs, before choosing AI.
items.vi: Đề xuất phương án thay thế.

items.en: I therefore recommend a conditional deployment: {MEASURE}.
items.vi: Khuyến nghị có điều kiện.

items.en: {ACTOR} remains accountable; the system should be suspended if {TRIGGER}.
items.vi: Ai chịu trách nhiệm + điều kiện dừng.

items.en: This choice has a cost — slower processing and higher operating expenses — but it protects {VALUE}, which I consider more important here than efficiency alone.
items.vi: Thừa nhận đánh đổi (trade-off).

usecases.title: Algorithmic videosurveillance at large events
usecases.brief: Ministère de l’Intérieur wants cameras + AI to detect risks (crowd surges, abandoned bags, weapons) during large events and trigger rapid action.

slots.PURPOSE: detect risky events in crowds and trigger rapid intervention
slots.AFFECTED: everyone attending or passing through the event, especially groups already over-policed
slots.HARM: chilling effect on freedom of assembly and discriminatory targeting
slots.VALUE: freedom of movement and assembly together with public safety
slots.AIACT: prohibited if it performs real-time remote biometric identification for law enforcement (outside narrow exceptions), and otherwise likely high-risk (law enforcement / biometrics, Annex III)
slots.DATA: images of identifiable people in public spaces
slots.WORKERS: annotators who labelled “suspicious behaviour” videos and operators watching alerts
slots.CONTEST: a complaint channel to the CNIL and a published register of alerts and interventions
slots.MEASURE: event detection only (no facial identification), limited zones and durations, a DPIA and FRIA, public signage, logs, independent audit of false alerts
slots.ALT: more stewards, better crowd-flow design and classic CCTV with trained staff
slots.CASE: Clearview AI and the Olympics experiment debates
slots.TRIGGER: false-alert rates differ across groups or the system is used beyond its declared zones and events
slots.WIDE: “mass surveillance of public space by the State”

angles: GDPR / Law Enforcement Directive (2016/680) for police purposes; proportionality and necessity
AI Act Art. 5 real-time RBI prohibition vs event detection
Deployer public body → FRIA (Art. 27), registration, human oversight
Workers who label “suspicious” behaviour define what counts as risk
Framing: safety vs liberty; reactivity of crowds aware of cameras

usecases.title: Consumer credit scoring with a human adviser
usecases.brief: A bank uses AI to score creditworthiness; the score is sent to an adviser who “decides”.

slots.PURPOSE: assess customers’ creditworthiness before granting loans
slots.AFFECTED: loan applicants, especially those with atypical income histories
slots.VALUE: equal access to an essential service
slots.AIACT: high-risk (Annex III, access to essential private services — credit)
slots.CONTEST: a written reasoned explanation and a review by a senior credit officer with power to overturn
slots.MEASURE: bias audits by group, input restrictions, logged adviser overrides, explanation letters and an independent appeal
slots.ALT: a transparent rules-based scorecard plus adviser judgment
slots.TRIGGER: advisers follow the score in almost all cases or refusal rates diverge across groups
slots.WIDE: “deciding who accesses credit as an essential service”

angles: SCHUFA trap: adviser rubber-stamping = automated decision

usecases.title: Automated CV screening (HR recruitment)
usecases.brief: A retail group (the course exercise uses Casino) wants AI to process CVs, evaluate candidates and filter applications.

slots.AFFECTED: job candidates, especially women, older and foreign-trained applicants
slots.HARM: discrimination reproduced from past hiring data
slots.AIACT: high-risk (Annex III, employment and workers management)
slots.WORKERS: annotators who tagged CV fields and “good candidate” labels
slots.CONTEST: the right to request human review and the reasons for rejection
slots.MEASURE: recruiters review a sample of rejected CVs, bias tests by group, no emotion or video analysis, notices to candidates
slots.ALT: structured blind screening by recruiters with a simple keyword filter
slots.CASE: Amazon’s abandoned recruiting tool and Gender Shades

angles: Appropriate human control measures (the class exercise question)
Emotion recognition at work is prohibited

usecases.title: Welfare-fraud risk scoring (CAF / SyRI)
usecases.brief: A benefits agency scores recipients to target fraud inspections.

slots.AFFECTED: benefit recipients — precarious, single-parent and disabled households
slots.DECISION: who is inspected and whose benefits are suspended
slots.VALUE: dignity and equal treatment of vulnerable people
slots.AIACT: high-risk (Annex III, access to essential public services and benefits); social scoring is prohibited
slots.WORKERS: caseworkers who label past fraud cases
slots.CONTEST: notification of the scoring, access to reasons and an appeal with suspension of sanctions
slots.MEASURE: publish the criteria, remove proxies for vulnerability, FRIA, independent audit and annual public report
slots.ALT: random plus rule-based inspections and simpler declaration forms
slots.TRIGGER: inspections concentrate on vulnerable groups without higher detected fraud
slots.WIDE: “which fraud we choose to look for (welfare fraud rather than company fraud)”

angles: Framing: focusing on welfare fraud is a normative choice
Collective contestation (La Quadrature du Net, Défenseur des droits)

usecases.title: Recidivism / pre-trial risk score (COMPAS-like)
usecases.brief: A justice ministry considers a risk score to help judges decide on release.

slots.PURPOSE: support judges’ release and sentencing decisions
slots.AFFECTED: defendants, disproportionately from minority and poor groups
slots.HARM: unequal error rates and loss of liberty
slots.VALUE: due process and the presumption of innocence
slots.AIACT: high-risk (administration of justice / law enforcement); prediction of crime solely from profiling is prohibited
slots.WORKERS: clerks who coded past case files
slots.CONTEST: disclosure of the score and its factors to the defence, with the right to challenge it in court

examMocks.title: Paper A — the official sample questions (fully written model answers)

questions.prompt: Name 5 different roles of actors in the AI sociotechnical system and how they contribute to AI.
questions.answer: A sociotechnical system links technical objects and people. (1) Researchers/developers design models and choose objectives. (2) Data workers (trainers, verifiers, imitators — Tubaro 2020) produce and check the data. (3) Companies/providers place systems on the market under their name and set business goals. (4) Deployers and users (judges, advisers, journalists) apply outputs — or resist them. (5) Regulators and standard bodies (AI Office, CNIL) set and enforce rules; affected people and NGOs contest decisions.

questions.prompt: Describe (in a few lines) an example of a value chain of annotation work.
questions.answer: Example: a French retail start-up sells “automatic” checkout cameras. It contracts a platform/BPO, which subcontracts to a firm in Madagascar. There, French-speaking graduates on day-rated contracts (≈ $0.4–1.7/h) label tray images and even watch live streams (impersonation). Several QA layers check accuracy before data return to the client’s ML team. Value is captured at the top while costs and opacity — “black boxes within black boxes” (Schmidt 2022) — are pushed down the chain.

questions.prompt: Give three methods used to analyse a sociotechnical system.
questions.answer: Analysing a sociotechnical system starts with framing where it begins and ends. (1) Ethnography and on-site interviews: observe what people actually do (e.g. Christin’s study of judges and journalists). (2) Discourse analysis: study how charters, press and laws describe AI. (3) Computational methods: network analysis/NLP, e.g. Gargiulo et al.’s map of 139M papers with community detection. Others: studying controversies, sociotechnical imaginaries, comparing press/science/regulation.

questions.prompt: Distinguish the trainer, the verifier and the imitator.
questions.answer: Tubaro, Casilli & Coville (2020) show three human roles behind AI. (1) The trainer prepares data: generating voice/image data and annotating it before training. (2) The verifier checks and corrects outputs of a live system (e.g. ASR transcripts), producing fresh labels — this never disappears. (3) The imitator replaces the algorithm and pretends to be AI (“artificial artificial intelligence”), e.g. Google Duplex calls made by humans.

questions.prompt: The French government asks for your expertise on the different trends in AI ethics and how they articulate. Provide a report of the topics they should look into, why they are relevant, and how they are positioned in the social world of AI.

plan.label: F
plan.text: AI ethics is not a single doctrine but a contested space in which actors frame “AI risk” differently. I frame it sociotechnically and map the trends using the four arenas of Benbouzid et al. (2020) and the three discursive poles of Gornet et al. (2024), choosing to prioritise present and unevenly distributed harms.

plan.label: A1
plan.text: Super-intelligence and AI safety: led by tech leaders (Musk, Altman), some academics (Hinton, Bengio) and philosophers (Bostrom), North-America-centred, it frames AI like nuclear technology. It matters because it has captured policymaker attention (Bletchley, AI safety institutes, AI Act code of practice). Its limit, according to Bender et al. (2021), is that hypothetical long-term risks distract from current harms. The government should follow it without letting it set the whole agenda.

plan.label: A2
plan.text: Technical and economic conformity: the open-world agents arena (Asilomar 2009) and the EU’s market approach see AI as a certifiable component — the AI Act, harmonised standards, CE marking, the Brussels effect. This trend is where most binding rules now come from. But certifying fundamental rights through standards is difficult, because rights depend on context and on judges (Gornet & Maxwell).

plan.label: A3
plan.text: Sociotechnical criticism: AI reinforces power structures (Weizenbaum) and has systematic bias (Buolamwini & Gebru); cases like SyRI, CNAF and Clearview show it. Ethics charters converge on five words — transparency, fairness, non-maleficence, responsibility, privacy (Jobin 2019) — but interpret them differently and omit work, power and ecology. The government should therefore look at hidden labour (Tubaro 2020) and materiality (Crawford 2021).

plan.label: R
plan.text: Recommendation: fund independent, interdisciplinary research; require operationalisation (owner, evidence, remedy) of every principle; involve affected groups and data workers. Trade-off: this is slower than relying on industry self-regulation, but soft law without enforcement risks “ethics washing”.

questions.prompt: The Ministère de l’Intérieur wants to deploy algorithmic videosurveillance at large-scale events to identify risks quickly. Identify the main legal issues, explain whether and how it is subject to the AI Act, and which measures it should take.

plan.label: F
plan.text: The Ministry wants AI on cameras to detect risks in crowds. I frame it not as “anomaly-detection accuracy” but as State surveillance of public space, and I prioritise freedom of assembly together with safety.

plan.label: A1
plan.text: Data protection: images of identifiable people are personal data. For police purposes the Law Enforcement Directive applies (the GDPR for other purposes): a legal basis in law, necessity and proportionality, purpose and storage limitation, a DPIA, and information to the public (signage). Measures: limit the zones and the duration to the event, define precise categories of events, delete footage quickly and keep logs.

plan.label: A2
plan.text: AI Act: the system infers alerts from video, so it is an AI system and the Ministry is a deployer (or a provider if it develops it). Real-time remote biometric identification in public spaces for law enforcement is prohibited except for narrow cases (Art. 5), so the system must detect events, not identify faces. As a law-enforcement or biometric use it is likely high-risk (Annex III), so: human oversight (Art. 14), logs, following the instructions of use, a FRIA as a public body (Art. 27) and registration.

plan.label: A3
plan.text: Effective oversight and contestation: under SCHUFA logic, an operator who always confirms alerts is not oversight. Operators need training, time and the authority to dismiss alerts, and their override rates should be audited. The “suspicious” labels come from annotators, whose choices define what counts as risk, so the training data must be audited for bias against particular groups. Citizens need a complaint route (CNIL) and published statistics.

plan.label: R
plan.text: I recommend a limited, time-bound experiment: event detection only, an independent evaluation and suspension if false alerts are unequal. Cost: less automation and more staff, which is justified by fundamental rights.

questions.prompt: OpenAI provided a purely technical document (fairness metrics, explainability algorithms, model weights and code) on how its LLM will be fair, accountable and transparent. Give the Commission guidelines to evaluate it critically.

plan.label: F
plan.text: The document frames trustworthiness as a technical property of the model. I adopt a sociotechnical framing and a normative choice: accountability towards the people affected, not only the technical correctness of the model.

plan.label: A1
plan.text: Question the purpose before the metric. The mulching proposal (Keyes et al., 2019) shows that FAT can make an unacceptable system look “fair”. Guideline: ask what the LLM will be used for, by whom and on whom, and which alternatives were considered. Any fairness metric is a normative choice, and it should be intersectional rather than limited to a single attribute.

plan.label: A2
plan.text: Transparency for whom? Model weights and code help experts but not citizens. Explanations must be selective and contrastive (Miller), and adapted to laypeople and regulators. Guideline: demand usable documentation (capabilities, limits, training-data summary, copyright policy — the GPAI duties), incident reporting and evaluation of systemic risks, and a channel for contestation.

plan.label: A3
plan.text: Accountability covers what is missing from the document: the RLHF raters and moderators (trainers and verifiers, Tubaro 2020), their contracts and pay; energy and water use (Crawford); and who is liable when outputs harm someone (Air Canada). Guideline: put audit rights, worker conditions and liability in the contract.

plan.label: R
plan.text: The Commission should evaluate with a checklist covering purpose, affected people, contestation, workers, materiality and liability, and suspend the partnership if information is refused. The trade-off is a longer procurement process, but it avoids pure “ethics washing”.

questions.prompt: The Commission is setting up an independent scientific panel to support the implementation and enforcement of the AI Act. Recommend which expertises it should include, and why, and how it should be balanced.

plan.label: F
plan.text: The panel must be scientific (research-based) and independent from the Commission, so Commission staff and non-researchers are out of scope. Every composition implies a framing of AI, so I choose a sociotechnical framing that makes this choice explicit.

plan.label: A1
plan.text: Technical coverage: AI is not linear — symbolic, connectionist and neuro-symbolic approaches coexist (Cardon et al., 2018). Gargiulo et al. (2023) map the field into theoretical areas (machine learning, neural networks, expert systems) and application areas (NLP, computer vision). I would use their publication shares to balance part of the panel, plus experts in GPAI evaluation, since the panel can issue qualified alerts on systemic risk.

plan.label: A2
plan.text: Social science coverage: AI ethics and AI safety frame risk differently, so both should be represented. Sociologists and anthropologists of AI can show usage issues such as decoupling that hinder enforcement. Legal scholars can work on standards and fundamental rights. Design researchers can check that explanation and contestation mechanisms are realistic. Members should have AI-specific expertise, not just a general discipline.

plan.label: A3
plan.text: Balance and independence: declare and manage industry conflicts of interest (rarely treated as COI in AI), balance gender and geography (not only North-American safety voices), and include researchers on labour and the environment, which charters often omit.

plan.label: R
plan.text: The result is an interdisciplinary panel with weighted technical seats and a social-science core, with public conflict-of-interest declarations and periodic rotation. The cost is a slower consensus, but it gives a broader and more legitimate view of AI risks.

questions.prompt: A retail group wants an AI tool that automatically processes CVs, evaluates candidates and filters applications. What would be appropriate human control measures, and what else should it consider?

plan.label: F
plan.text: The tool shapes access to employment. I frame it as a hiring process, not only as a matching model, and I prioritise non-discrimination.

plan.label: A1
plan.text: Classification: an AI system used for recruitment is high-risk (Annex III, employment). The provider must ensure risk management, data governance against historical bias (Art. 10), documentation and logs. The group, as deployer, must follow the instructions of use, inform candidates and workers’ representatives, and organise human oversight. Emotion recognition in video interviews is prohibited at work.

plan.label: A2
plan.text: Human control must be real: recruiters review a random sample of rejected CVs, can override without penalty, have the time and the reasons, and their override rate is monitored. Under SCHUFA, rubber-stamping makes the rejection an automated decision under Art. 22 GDPR, which gives rights to human intervention and contestation.

plan.label: A3
plan.text: Hidden labour and data: CV fields and “good hire” labels were annotated by workers whose instructions define the ground truth (Miceli & Posada). The group should ask the vendor who labelled the data, how and at what pay, and test selection rates by gender, age and origin, including intersections.

plan.label: R
plan.text: I recommend a pilot in which the AI only sorts and never rejects alone, with bias audits and stopping if selection rates diverge. Cost: slower screening, but fairer access to jobs.

questions.prompt: A benefits agency presents its new fraud-scoring algorithm as “a neutral efficiency tool”. Analyse this framing and propose an alternative framing.

plan.label: F
plan.text: Framing decides where the system starts and ends. Calling the algorithm “neutral efficiency” frames it as a technical optimisation; I propose to frame it as a policy choice about whom the State controls, and I prioritise equal dignity.

plan.label: A1
plan.text: What the efficiency framing hides: the choice to target welfare fraud rather than tax or company fraud is already normative. It shows the model’s accuracy but hides the affected households, the caseworkers who labelled past cases, and the political decision. Cases such as SyRI and CNAF show the consequences: inspections concentrated on the poorest, which compounds injustice (Eidelson).

plan.label: A2
plan.text: Reactivity and technosolutionism: once people are scored, recipients and inspectors adapt to the score (Espeland & Sauder), and a fair metric can still serve an unjust purpose (Kalluri, the mulching lesson). The agency must justify why AI is necessary at all compared with simpler forms and random checks.

plan.label: A3
plan.text: Consequences for law and contestation: as essential public benefits, the system is high-risk (social scoring is prohibited), so a FRIA is required. Affected people need notification, reasons and an appeal, but individual appeals do not fix information asymmetry, so the agency should publish statistics and allow NGOs and the Défenseur des droits to scrutinise it.

plan.label: R
plan.text: Under the alternative framing, deployment is conditional on public debate, published criteria and stopping if inspections target vulnerable groups without more fraud being detected. Cost: less “efficiency”, but more legitimacy.

examMocks.title: Paper B — law, users and generative AI (outline answers)

questions.prompt: What is soft law? Give two of its shortcomings.
questions.answer: Soft law is a set of non-binding agreements, principles and declarations (e.g. ethics charters, OECD principles), unlike hard law, which is enforceable in court. Shortcomings: (1) it has no effect without voluntary adherence; (2) it lacks legal security and can bypass democratic institutions — a way to avoid strict regulation. It can, however, harden, for example when a company publicly commits to it and the CNIL/FTC enforces that commitment.

questions.prompt: Name four AI practices prohibited by the AI Act.
questions.answer: Article 5 of the AI Act prohibits “unacceptable-risk” practices, including: (1) social scoring; (2) emotion inference in the workplace or in education; (3) untargeted scraping of facial images to build recognition databases; (4) real-time remote biometric identification in public spaces for law enforcement, apart from narrow exceptions (missing persons, terrorism…). Others: subliminal manipulation, exploiting vulnerabilities, crime prediction from profiling. Fines can reach €35M or 7% of turnover.

questions.prompt: Define decoupling and buffering.
questions.answer: Decoupling (Meyer & Rowan, 1977) is the separation between management discourse (“the algorithm is deployed”) and employees’ actual practice. Buffering is how workers protect their work from algorithms: (1) foot-dragging — ignoring the tool or putting its results at the end of reports; (2) gaming — clickbait titles, choosing cases; (3) open critique. Christin observed both among judges and web journalists.

questions.prompt: What does the COMPAS case teach about AI bias?
questions.answer: COMPAS is a US recidivism score that ProPublica (2016) showed had unequal errors between Black and white defendants. Lessons: (1) it moved a technical debate into the public sphere; (2) data science and criminology talked past each other; (3) choosing a fairness metric is a normative choice; (4) the deeper question is whether the detention practice itself is just (Kalluri: ask how AI shifts power).

questions.prompt: A bank uses an AI credit score that is sent to an adviser who formally decides. Is this an automated decision? What should the bank do?

plan.label: F
plan.text: Framing: access to credit as an essential service, not only default prediction. Value: equal access.

plan.label: A1
plan.text: SCHUFA trap: if the score decisively drives the adviser, it is an automated decision under Art. 22 GDPR, which gives rights to human intervention, to express a view and to contest.

plan.label: A2
plan.text: AI Act high-risk (credit, Annex III): the bank as deployer ensures oversight and logs, and as provider if it develops in-house; data governance; FRIA for credit scoring.

plan.label: A3
plan.text: Users: advisers under sales targets may rubber-stamp (decoupling). Measure the override rate, give time and authority, and send explanation letters adapted to customers.

plan.label: R
plan.text: Conditional use with an audited override rate and stopping if refusal rates diverge; cost: slower decisions.

questions.prompt: A public service launches an LLM chatbot to answer citizens. Identify the legal and ethical issues and propose safeguards.

plan.label: F
plan.text: An information service to citizens; value: reliable, accountable information.

plan.label: A1
plan.text: Transparency (Art. 50): disclose the AI and mark generated content; GDPR for the prompts (minimisation, retention, processor contract).

plan.label: A2
plan.text: Liability: a wrong answer can bind the institution (Air Canada); a disclaimer is not enough → verified sources, escalation to a human.

plan.label: A3
plan.text: GPAI underneath: downstream information duties, copyright policy; hidden RLHF/moderation workers; energy costs.

plan.label: R
plan.text: Bounded release on low-stakes topics, human escalation and incident logs; stop if repeated harmful answers occur.

questions.prompt: A cloud provider claims its AI service is “immaterial and green”. How should a public buyer assess this claim?

plan.label: F
plan.text: Rematerialise the cloud (Crawford): chips, mines, energy, water, labour.

plan.label: A1
plan.text: Ask for the system boundary: training + repeated inference + hardware + data centres; the electricity mix; the period (Luccioni et al. on BLOOM).

plan.label: A2
plan.text: Deep learning is not always better (Delarue 2024): compare with frugal/no-AI alternatives; beware of rebound effects.

plan.label: A3
plan.text: Labour materiality: annotation and verification chains in the Global South; data colonialism.

plan.label: R
plan.text: Procurement criteria with measured footprints and independent verification; the trade-off may be lower performance.

questions.prompt: Managers say a decision-support algorithm is “successfully deployed”, but staff seem not to use it. Design a study to find out what happens.

plan.label: F
plan.text: The gap between discourse and practice is an empirical question (decoupling).

plan.label: A1
plan.text: Methods: ethnography of daily work, interviews with staff and managers, analysis of usage logs (computational).

plan.label: A2
plan.text: What to look for: buffering (foot-dragging, gaming, open critique), the misalignment of the algorithm’s goals with professional goals, algorithmic imaginaries (Bucher).

plan.label: A3
plan.text: Interpret through expert fields: barriers to entry, identity, attitude to technology (judges vs journalists).

plan.label: R
plan.text: Results feed a redesign or withdrawal; resistance is information, not irrationality.

questions.prompt: Design a meaningful contestation mechanism for people refused a public benefit by an algorithmic system.

plan.label: F
plan.text: Contestability = the political turn of explainability; value: dignity of the vulnerable.

plan.label: A1
plan.text: Individual: a contrastive, plain-language explanation, access to data, the correction of errors, a reviewer with authority to overturn and suspension of the sanction during review (Art. 22(3)).

plan.label: A2
plan.text: Usability for both sides: not a 50-page report, not a postal letter at midnight; offline and assisted channels for low digital literacy.

plan.label: A3
plan.text: Collective: aggregated complaint statistics, the Défenseur des droits, NGOs (La Quadrature du Net), public deliberation (contestation matrix; Alfrink et al.).

plan.label: R
plan.text: Link appeals to system redesign; the cost is administrative time.

questions.prompt: Does ChatGPT pose a systemic risk under the AI Act? Build a short risk assessment.

plan.label: F
plan.text: GPAI model vs downstream system; systemic risk is defined legally.

plan.label: A1
plan.text: Criteria: high-impact capabilities, presumption > 10^25 FLOPs or Commission designation (including a scientific-panel alert).

plan.label: A2
plan.text: Risks rated gravity × probability: personal data leaks, disinformation, harmful advice to vulnerable people, cyberattacks.

plan.label: A3
plan.text: Mitigations: evaluations and red-teaming, incident reporting to the AI Office, cybersecurity, plus the duties of downstream providers.

plan.label: R
plan.text: Likely systemic; remaining uncertainty about measuring capabilities.

examMocks.title: Paper C — labour, arenas and copyright (outline answers)

questions.prompt: What is the key criterion of an “AI system” in the AI Act?
questions.answer: Under the AI Act, an AI system is a machine-based system that, for explicit or implicit objectives, infers from its input how to generate outputs (predictions, content, recommendations, decisions) that can influence environments. The key criterion is the capacity to infer (machine learning or logic/knowledge-based). Autonomy and adaptiveness are optional; software executing rules defined solely by humans is excluded (Recital 12).

questions.prompt: Name four lawful bases of the GDPR and explain the “OR / AND” rule.
questions.answer: Article 6 GDPR: (1) consent, (2) performance of a contract, (3) legal obligation, (4) public interest/task — also vital interest and legitimate interest. Rule: each processing needs ONE lawful basis (“OR”) AND must respect ALL the Article 5 principles (“AND”): lawfulness, fairness and transparency; purpose limitation; minimisation; accuracy; storage limitation; integrity and confidentiality; accountability.

questions.prompt: According to Jobin et al. (2019), on which principles do AI ethics guidelines converge?
questions.answer: Jobin, Ienca & Vayena (2019) read 84 AI ethics guidelines and found 11 themes. Global convergence on five: (1) transparency, (2) justice and fairness, (3) non-maleficence, (4) responsibility, (5) privacy. But there is substantive divergence in how they are interpreted and implemented (polysemy), and topics such as work, power and ecology are missing.

questions.prompt: For whom and why do we explain AI decisions?
questions.answer: For whom: (1) experts, (2) laypeople, (3) regulators — each needs a different form. Why: descriptive (what the model does), explanatory (how), normative (justifying the decision) and contestable (giving grounds to challenge). Good explanations are selective, contrastive and dialogic (Miller), ideally producing a complexity drop (Dessalles).

questions.prompt: Brief a parliamentary committee on the difference between “AI safety” and “AI ethics”.

plan.label: F
plan.text: Two arenas framing risk differently; a framing defines which harms get attention.

plan.label: A1
plan.text: AI safety: existential / loss-of-control risk, led by tech leaders and some academics, North-America-centred, nuclear analogy → technology-centred rules (Bletchley, AI safety institutes).

plan.label: A2
plan.text: AI ethics / sociotechnical criticism: present harms, bias (Gender Shades), power (Weizenbaum), labour and ecology; tools: audits, social science.

plan.label: A3
plan.text: Overlaps and critiques: TESCREAL (Gebru & Torres), distraction from current harms (Bender); but safety research also covers short-term robustness.

plan.label: R
plan.text: The committee should fund both, but target present harms with enforceable rules.

questions.prompt: A French company outsources image annotation to a BPO in Madagascar. Write procurement guidelines.

plan.label: F
plan.text: Value chain and multilayer stacks: accuracy targets push costs down the chain.

plan.label: A1
plan.text: Visibility: list every subcontractor and audit rights; avoid “black boxes within black boxes”.

plan.label: A2
plan.text: Conditions: effective hourly pay including unpaid time, contract type (not day-rated without leave), paid training, psychological support for harmful content.

plan.label: A3
plan.text: Instructions–interface–metrics: allow workers to flag ambiguous labels; ground truth is co-produced; dispute procedures.

plan.label: R
plan.text: Price floors and monitoring; the cost is higher, but the data are better and the work decent.

questions.prompt: An LLM provider trained on publicly accessible books and websites. Discuss copyright in the EU and the US.

plan.label: F
plan.text: Copyright protects original human expression in a fixed medium; ideas are not protected.

plan.label: A1
plan.text: EU: TDM exceptions — research (Art. 3) and general with opt-out (Art. 4); lawful access required; public ≠ free.

plan.label: A2
plan.text: US: fair use with four factors (transformative?, nature, amount, market effect); a separate doctrine.

plan.label: A3
plan.text: AI Act GPAI duties: copyright policy respecting opt-outs + public training-content summary, which still apply even to open models; output filtering; machine output is not protected.

plan.label: R
plan.text: Recommend licensing and opt-out compliance; trade-off with data scale.

questions.prompt: A court builds an in-house AI to anonymise its decisions (Cour de cassation). What does this case teach about AI work and users?

plan.label: F
plan.text: Internal data work by civil servants (typology: internal, employees).

plan.label: A1
plan.text: Training never ends: a permanent team, verification as a strategic need.

plan.label: A2
plan.text: The AI as an “absent colleague”, called “the software”; annotators use empathy to keep decisions readable.

plan.label: A3
plan.text: Pseudonymisation vs anonymisation; there is a trade-off between readability and protection.

plan.label: R
plan.text: Budget permanent staff and recognise their work in the system’s design.

questions.prompt: A city wants “AI to solve homelessness”. Critically assess this proposal.

plan.label: F
plan.text: Technosolutionism: assuming technology is a necessary part of the solution.

plan.label: A1
plan.text: Post-hoc rationalisation; the real problem may be housing policy (tech neutrality vs tech politics).

plan.label: A2
plan.text: Mulching lesson: making it fair and transparent does not make the purpose legitimate.

plan.label: A3
plan.text: Who is affected and can they contest? Data colonialism of vulnerable people; reactivity of indicators.

plan.label: R
plan.text: Start from the need with the people affected; AI only if it is proven proportionate.

questions.prompt: A border agency adopts facial recognition. Discuss its classification and risks.

plan.label: F
plan.text: Power asymmetry at borders.

plan.label: A1
plan.text: AI Act: high-risk (migration/borders, biometrics); untargeted face scraping prohibited (Clearview).

plan.label: A2

chapters.title: 6 · GDPR and the human in the loop

nodes.label: Framing
nodes.en: Choosing where a technical object starts and ends; it makes some problems, actors and remedies visible and hides others.
nodes.vi: Đóng khung: chọn ranh giới đối tượng phân tích — làm lộ ra cái này, che khuất cái kia.

nodes.label: Sociotechnical system
nodes.en: Models, data, workers, institutions, users, law and affected people studied as one system.
nodes.vi: Hệ thống xã hội–kỹ thuật: công nghệ và con người là một khối.

nodes.label: STS methods
nodes.en: Ethnography/interviews, discourse analysis, computational methods, controversies, imaginaries.
nodes.vi: Phương pháp: dân tộc học, phân tích diễn ngôn, phương pháp tính toán, tranh cãi.

nodes.label: Polysemy of AI
nodes.en: AI means different things in technical, media, regulatory and scientific arenas.
nodes.vi: AI đa nghĩa tuỳ đấu trường.

nodes.label: Symbolic vs connectionist
nodes.en: Rival, coexisting traditions; history of AI is not linear (Cardon 2018, Gargiulo 2023).
nodes.vi: Biểu tượng vs nơ-ron: cùng tồn tại, lịch sử không tuyến tính.

nodes.label: Materiality of AI
nodes.en: AI depends on minerals, energy, water, hardware and labour (Crawford).
nodes.vi: Tính vật chất: khoáng sản, điện, nước, phần cứng, lao động.

nodes.label: Hidden human labour
nodes.en: Human work behind “automatic” AI that is made invisible.
nodes.vi: Lao động con người bị che giấu sau AI “tự động”.

nodes.label: Data colonialism
nodes.en: Extraction of value from data concentrating wealth; extension of colonialism and capitalism.
nodes.vi: Thực dân dữ liệu: khai thác giá trị, tập trung của cải.

nodes.label: Reactivity / quantification
nodes.en: People adapt to what is measured, so measures reshape the world (Espeland & Sauder).
nodes.vi: Tính phản ứng: con người chạy theo chỉ số đo.

nodes.label: Shifting power
nodes.en: Ask who gains and loses power, not only whether AI is fair (Kalluri).
nodes.vi: Hỏi: ai được/mất quyền lực?

nodes.label: Hype
nodes.en: Mismatch between claims and reality; waves of hope and hype.
nodes.vi: Thổi phồng: lời hứa ≠ thực tế.

nodes.label: Ethics charters
nodes.en: 84–436 guidelines converging on 5 principles but divergent in meaning (Jobin; Gornet).
nodes.vi: Hiến chương đạo đức: hội tụ 5 nguyên tắc, hiểu khác nhau.

nodes.label: Three poles of discourse
nodes.en: Technical, regulatory and business/innovation discourses.
nodes.vi: Ba cực: kỹ thuật, pháp lý, kinh doanh.

nodes.label: Operationalisation gap
nodes.en: Principles rarely become concrete procedures; work, power and ecology stay invisible.
nodes.vi: Khoảng trống vận hành hoá: nguyên tắc chưa thành quy trình.

nodes.label: Four arenas
nodes.en: Super-intelligence, open-world agents, sociotechnical criticism, technical-economic conformity.
nodes.vi: Bốn đấu trường đóng khung rủi ro khác nhau.

nodes.label: AI safety arena
nodes.en: Existential/loss-of-control framing led by tech leaders; nuclear analogy.
nodes.vi: An toàn AI: rủi ro tồn vong, so sánh hạt nhân.

nodes.label: Sociotechnical criticism
nodes.en: AI reinforces power structures and carries systematic bias; audits and social science.
nodes.vi: Phê phán xã hội–kỹ thuật: quyền lực, thiên lệch hệ thống.

nodes.label: Conformity / Brussels effect
nodes.en: EU market approach: build conformity for AI products; rules spread globally.
nodes.vi: Tuân thủ thị trường EU, hiệu ứng Brussels.

nodes.label: Harmonised standards
nodes.en: Technical norms giving presumption of conformity; hard to certify fundamental rights.
nodes.vi: Tiêu chuẩn hài hoà; khó “chứng nhận” quyền con người.

nodes.label: Soft law
nodes.en: Non-binding principles; can harden through public commitment or binding texts.
nodes.vi: Luật mềm: không ràng buộc nhưng có thể “cứng lại”.

nodes.label: GDPR basis + principles
nodes.en: One lawful basis AND all Art. 5 principles; accountability.
nodes.vi: GDPR: một cơ sở pháp lý VÀ mọi nguyên tắc.

nodes.label: Pseudonymisation
nodes.en: Data with identifiers replaced remain personal data.
nodes.vi: Giả danh hoá vẫn là dữ liệu cá nhân.

nodes.label: Art. 22 GDPR
nodes.en: Right not to be subject to solely automated decisions with significant effects; right to contest.
nodes.vi: Quyền không bị quyết định hoàn toàn tự động.

nodes.label: SCHUFA ruling
nodes.en: A score that decisively drives a human’s decision is an automated decision (CJEU 2023).
nodes.vi: Án SCHUFA: con người đóng dấu điểm máy = quyết định tự động.

nodes.label: DPIA / FRIA
nodes.en: Impact assessments: data protection (GDPR Art. 35) and fundamental rights (AI Act Art. 27).
nodes.vi: Đánh giá tác động: dữ liệu (DPIA) và quyền cơ bản (FRIA).

nodes.label: AI system (definition)
nodes.en: Machine-based system that infers outputs from inputs; inference is the key criterion.
nodes.vi: Định nghĩa hệ thống AI: tiêu chí suy luận.

nodes.label: Provider / deployer
nodes.en: Who places the system on the market vs who uses it; duties follow the role.
nodes.vi: Nhà cung cấp / bên triển khai: nghĩa vụ theo vai trò.

nodes.label: Risk pyramid
nodes.en: Prohibited, high-risk, transparency, minimal; plus GPAI rules.
nodes.vi: Kim tự tháp rủi ro.

nodes.label: Prohibited practices
nodes.en: Social scoring, emotion inference at work/school, real-time RBI for police, face scraping…
nodes.vi: Thực hành bị cấm.

nodes.label: High-risk obligations
nodes.en: Risk management, data governance, documentation, logs, oversight, robustness (Art. 9–17).
nodes.vi: Nghĩa vụ hệ rủi ro cao.

nodes.label: Human oversight (Art. 14)
nodes.en: People must be able to understand, monitor, override and stop the system.
nodes.vi: Giám sát của con người: hiểu, theo dõi, bác bỏ, dừng.

nodes.label: Transparency (Art. 50)
nodes.en: Disclose AI interaction, mark synthetic content, disclose deepfakes.
nodes.vi: Minh bạch: báo là AI, đánh dấu nội dung tổng hợp.

nodes.label: GPAI model
nodes.en: General-purpose model integrable downstream; documentation, copyright policy, training summary.
nodes.vi: Mô hình AI đa dụng.

nodes.label: Systemic risk
nodes.en: High-impact GPAI risk; presumed above 10^25 FLOPs or designated.
nodes.vi: Rủi ro hệ thống của GPAI.

nodes.label: AI Office & scientific panel
nodes.en: EU enforcement of GPAI; independent experts can issue qualified alerts.
nodes.vi: Văn phòng AI và hội đồng khoa học độc lập.

nodes.label: Copyright & TDM
nodes.en: Protects human expression; EU TDM exceptions with opt-out vs US fair use.
nodes.vi: Bản quyền và ngoại lệ khai thác dữ liệu.

nodes.label: Liability
nodes.en: Contractual, civil (fault + harm + causation), product, criminal; disclaimers are not enough.
nodes.vi: Trách nhiệm pháp lý.

nodes.label: Platform
nodes.en: Intermediary that matches parties, captures data and taskifies contributions.
nodes.vi: Nền tảng trung gian.

nodes.label: Taskification
nodes.en: Breaking work into standardised micro-tasks.
nodes.vi: Nhiệm vụ hoá.

nodes.label: Digital labour
nodes.en: Continuum from unpaid user activity to micro-paid piecework.
nodes.vi: Lao động số.

nodes.label: Trainer / verifier / imitator
nodes.en: Three human roles behind AI (Tubaro et al. 2020).
nodes.vi: Ba vai trò: huấn luyện, kiểm định, giả làm AI.

nodes.label: Value chain & multilayer stacks
nodes.en: Chains of subcontractors: “black boxes within black boxes” (Schmidt).
nodes.vi: Chuỗi giá trị nhiều tầng thầu phụ.

nodes.label: Data-production dispositif
nodes.en: Instructions + interface + metrics define “ground truth” and pace (Miceli & Posada).
nodes.vi: Bộ máy sản xuất dữ liệu quyết định “sự thật”.

nodes.label: Effective pay & conditions
nodes.en: Piece rate ≠ hourly pay; precarious contracts, harmful content.
nodes.vi: Thu nhập thực và điều kiện làm việc.

nodes.label: Global North–South division
nodes.en: Demand in North America/Europe, data work in the Global South.
nodes.vi: Phân công lao động Bắc–Nam.

nodes.label: Algorithmic bias (COMPAS)
nodes.en: Unequal errors; debiasing has mixed results; metric choice is normative.
nodes.vi: Thiên lệch thuật toán, vụ COMPAS.

nodes.label: Fair AI vs radical AI
nodes.en: A fair algorithm is pointless without deeper change (SyRI, CNAF, Clearview).
nodes.vi: AI công bằng vs AI cấp tiến.

nodes.label: Technosolutionism
nodes.en: Assuming technology is a necessary part of the solution.
nodes.vi: Chủ nghĩa giải pháp công nghệ.

nodes.label: Mulching proposal
nodes.en: Satire: FAT can make an unacceptable purpose look acceptable.
nodes.vi: Bài châm biếm “đề xuất nghiền”.

nodes.label: Decoupling & buffering
nodes.en: Gap between management discourse and practice; foot-dragging, gaming, critique.
nodes.vi: Tách rời diễn ngôn–thực hành; kháng cự.

nodes.label: Expert fields
nodes.en: Judges vs journalists react differently to algorithms (Christin; Bourdieu).
nodes.vi: Trường chuyên gia: thẩm phán vs nhà báo.

nodes.label: Cour de cassation
nodes.en: In-house anonymisation AI: training never ends, “absent colleague”.
nodes.vi: Toà Phá án: huấn luyện không bao giờ kết thúc.

nodes.label: Explanations
nodes.en: Selective, contrastive, dialogic; for experts, laypeople or regulators.
nodes.vi: Giải thích: chọn lọc, đối chiếu, theo người nghe.

nodes.label: Contestability
nodes.en: Ability to challenge and change an outcome; political turn of explainability.
nodes.vi: Khả năng phản đối/khiếu nại.

nodes.label: Collective contestation
nodes.en: NGOs, ombudsperson, public scrutiny tools address information asymmetry.
nodes.vi: Phản đối tập thể: NGO, Défenseur des droits, cơ sở dữ liệu công khai.

threads.title: Framing thread
threads.use: Any “analyse/critique this proposal” question — the teachers’ favourite.

steps.text: Start by saying where the system begins and ends: framing decides what is visible.
Choose a wide, sociotechnical framing: data, workers, institutions, users, affected people.
Show that actors frame the risk differently (safety, conformity, criticism).
Even a fairness metric is a framing choice — COMPAS.
Ask whether fixing the algorithm is enough, or whether the practice itself is unjust.
Question whether technology is needed at all.
Conclude: FAT checklists cannot justify an unacceptable purpose.

threads.title: Human-in-the-loop thread
threads.use: Credit, hiring, welfare, videosurveillance: “is there real human control?”

steps.text: Name the humans: AI depends on hidden labour.
Classify them: trainers, verifiers, imitators — who, contract, pay, internal or external.
Their instructions and metrics define the ground truth the model learns.
The AI Act requires oversight able to understand, override and stop.
But a reviewer who always follows the score is not oversight.
Then the decision is automated and Art. 22 safeguards apply.
Check in practice: measure override rates, observe use.
Give affected people a real way to challenge the outcome.

threads.title: From ethics to law thread
threads.use: Government report on AI ethics trends; “is a charter enough?”

steps.text: Charters converge on five principles but mean different things.
They lack operationalisation and omit work, power, ecology.
Legally they are soft law — binding only if they harden.
The EU hardened them into a market-conformity regulation.
The AI Act sorts systems into a risk pyramid.
High-risk systems get concrete obligations.
Standards operationalise them…
…but fundamental rights still need contextual impact assessments.

threads.title: Power & extraction thread
threads.use: Materiality, labour, Global South, “who benefits?” questions.

steps.text: Rematerialise the cloud: minerals, energy, labour.
Value is extracted from data and concentrated.
Work flows to the Global South, demand stays in the North.
Through multilayer subcontracting chains…
…that push costs and precarity down to workers.
So ask who gains and who loses power.
And give collective, not only individual, means to contest.
